dstask

Single binary terminal-based TODO manager with git-based sync + markdown notes per task




Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of a special protocol. If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge conflict, then dstask is for you! https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) ## Features - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! - Task listing won't break with long task text - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows - A single statically-linked binary - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. ## Non-features - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a multi-person project tracked elsewhere. ## Requirements - Git - A 256-color capable terminal ## Installation 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 1. Enable shell completions: - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` ## PowerShell completion Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: ```powershell dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' ``` ## Usage Run `dstask help` for usage information. ### Basic Commands - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on - `dstask start` - Start working on a task - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete - `dstask edit` - Edit a task - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote ### Task Properties - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved ### Contexts Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: ```bash dstask context work dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work dstask # shows only work tasks dstask context -- # clear context ``` ### Git Sync Sync your tasks across devices using git: ```bash # Set up sync on first device cd ~/.dstask git remote add origin git push -u origin master # On other devices git clone ~/.dstask # To sync dstask sync ``` ### Templates Create task templates for recurring patterns: ```bash dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 dstask add from-template ``` ## Best Practices - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context ## Database The default database location is: - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. ## Integration of fuzzy finders Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: ```bash function dstask () { local has_double_dash subcommand if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] then command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" return fi fi command dstask "$@" } ``` The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All other commands are passed directly to dstask. ## Alternatives Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy ## FAQ > Does dstask encrypt tasks? Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote repository encrypted, you may consider [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the tools themselves. > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? Yes. 1. Set a context: 2. Run a modify command without and ID 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. > Is there a GUI or web interface? Not as part of dstask itself. However, dstask can be used as a library -- @botto has started developing a web GUI, specifically to allow task management on-the-go via a smartphone: . It's in early stages but is meaningful as having no smartphone-based control is a blocker for a lot of people. > Has dstask been featured in a magazine? Yes! :-) [releases]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases --- dstask-import.md taskwarrior-migration.md

# dstask-import

usage: `dstask-import github|tw`

dstask-import is a tool to synchronize between external services or tools, and dstask.
At this point it supports importing from:

* taskwarrior
* GitHub

See below for details on each

## Taskwarrior

The import functionality is designed to aid with the transition from using taskwarrior to dstask.

Before installing dstask, you may want to export your taskwarrior database:

    task export > taskwarrior.json

After un-installing taskwarrior and installing dstask, to import the tasks to
dstask after initialising the dstask database with git:

    mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init
    dstask-import tw < taskwarrior.json

Note that the import process is lossy due to subtle differences between taskwarrior and dstask.

## GitHub

You can import issues from GitHub repositories into dstask.

### Authentication

To import from private repositories, you'll need a GitHub personal access token.
For public repositories, authentication is optional but recommended to avoid rate limits.

### Usage

To import issues from a GitHub repository:

    dstask-import github <owner>/<repo>

You can also import from multiple repositories by running the command multiple times.
# Moving from Taskwarrior

## Importing data

Please see the [dstask-import tw instructions](dstask-import.md#taskwarrior) to import taskwarrior tasks.

## Using dstask

Commands and syntax are deliberately very similar to taskwarrior. Here are the exceptions:

  * The command is (nearly) always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will. If there's an ID, it can proceed the command but doesn't have to.
  * Priorities are added by the keywords `P0` `P1` `P2` `P3`. Lower number is more urgent. Default is `P2`. For example `task add eat some bananas P1`. The keyword can be anywhere after the command.
  * Action is always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will.
  * Contexts are defined on-the-fly, and are added to all new tasks if set. Use `--` to ignore current context in any command.

[1]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases/latest

Usage: dstask [id...] <cmd> [task summary/filter]

Where [task summary] is text with tags/project/priority specified. Tags are
specified with + (or - for filtering) eg: +work. The project is specified with
a project:g prefix eg: project:dstask -- no quotes. Priorities run from P3
(low), P2 (default) to P1 (high) and P0 (critical). Text can also be specified
for a substring search of description and notes.

Cmd and IDs can be swapped, multiple IDs can be specified for batch
operations.

	echo "usage: $0 <ref> <oldrev> <newrev>" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# --- Config
allowunannotated=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowunannotated)
allowdeletebranch=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowdeletebranch)
denycreatebranch=$(git config --type=bool hooks.denycreatebranch)
allowdeletetag=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowdeletetag)
allowmodifytag=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowmodifytag)

case "$projectdesc" in
"Unnamed repository"* | "")
	echo "*** Project description file hasn't been set" >&2
	exit 1
	;;
esac

# --- Check types
# if $newrev is 0000...0000, it's a commit to delete a ref.
zero=$(git hash-object --stdin </dev/null | tr '[0-9a-f]' '0')
if [ "$newrev" = "$zero" ]; then
	newrev_type=delete
else
	newrev_type=$(git cat-file -t $newrev)
fi

case "$refname","$newrev_type" in
	refs/tags/*,commit)
		# un-annotated tag
		short_refname=${refname##refs/tags/}
		if [ "$allowunannotated" != "true" ]; then
			echo "*** The un-annotated tag, $short_refname, is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			echo "*** Use 'git tag [ -a | -s ]' for tags you want to propagate." >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/tags/*,delete)

		if [ "$allowdeletetag" != "true" ]; then
			echo "*** Deleting a tag is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/tags/*,tag)

		if [ "$allowmodifytag" != "true" ] && git rev-parse $refname > /dev/null 2>&1

			echo "*** Tag '$refname' already exists." >&2

Where [task summary] is text with tags/project/priority specified. Tags are

a project:g prefix eg: project:dstask -- no quotes. Priorities run from P3

_dstask() {
    # reconstruct COMP_WORDS to re-join separations caused by colon (which is a default separator)
    # yes, this method ends up splitting by spaces, but that's not a problem for the dstask parser
    # see http://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/bash/FAQ
    original_args=( $(echo "${COMP_WORDS[@]}" | sed 's/ : /:/g' | sed 's/ :$/:/g') )

    # hand to dstask as canonical args
    COMPREPLY=( $(dstask _completions "${original_args[@]}") )

    # convert dstask's suggestions to remove prefix before colon so complete can understand it
    local last_arg="${original_args[-1]}"
    local colon_word=${last_arg%"${last_arg##*:}"}
    local i=${#COMPREPLY[*]}
    while [[ $((--i)) -ge 0 ]]; do
        COMPREPLY[$i]=${COMPREPLY[$i]#"$colon_word"}
    done
}

# wire bash completions to dstask completion engine. Some of the workarounds for
# idiosyncrasies around separation with colons taken from /etc/bash_completion

_dstask() {
    # reconstruct COMP_WORDS to re-join separations caused by colon (which is a default separator)
    # yes, this method ends up splitting by spaces, but that's not a problem for the dstask parser
    # see http://tiswww.case.edu/php/chet/bash/FAQ
    original_args=( $(echo "${COMP_WORDS[@]}" | sed 's/ : /:/g' | sed 's/ :$/:/g') )

    # hand to dstask as canonical args
    COMPREPLY=( $(dstask _completions "${original_args[@]}") )

    # convert dstask's suggestions to remove prefix before colon so complete can understand it
    local last_arg="${original_args[-1]}"
    local colon_word=${last_arg%"${last_arg##*:}"}
    local i=${#COMPREPLY[*]}
    while [[ $((--i)) -ge 0 ]]; do
        COMPREPLY[$i]=${COMPREPLY[$i]#"$colon_word"}
    done
}

./executable show-open 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool

# modify: change tags, project, priority, due
./executable 1 modify +c -b project:proj2 P2 due:2025-12-02 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml

# modify clear project

cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml

# modify clear project with -project: ?
./executable 1 modify -project:proj2 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml
./executable add "task B" project:proj2 2>&1
./executable 2 modify -project:proj2 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml

# modify due clear?
./executable 1 modify due: 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml

# modify with multiple IDs
./executable add "task C" +x 2>&1
./executable 1 2 modify +y 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml

# modify without IDs - should affect context
./executable context +a 2>&1
./executable add "task D" +a 2>&1
./executable show-open 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "id|summary|tags"
printf "y\n" | ./executable modify +z 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml | grep tags -A2
./executable context none 2>&1

# Test filter parsing: does priority work as anti?
./executable add "prio test P1" 2>&1
./executable add "prio test2 P2" 2>&1
./executable show-open P1 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "id|summary|priority"
./executable show-open -P1 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "id|summary" || true

./executable show-open due:2025-12-02 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "id|summary|due"

./executable add "note search base" 2>&1
./executable 7 note "secretkeyword" 2>&1
./executable show-open secretkeyword 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|notes"

./executable show-open secret 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|notes"

./executable add "ctx proj test" 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/pending/*.yml | tail -n 30
./executable show-open 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|project"
./executable context none 2>&1
./executable show-open -- 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|project" | head -n 20

# Test DSTASK_CONTEXT env
DSTASK_CONTEXT="project:proj1" ./executable show-open 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|project"
DSTASK_CONTEXT="+a" ./executable show-open 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|tags"

# Test start adding task: dstask start "new task"
./executable start "started task" +started P0 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/active/*.yml | tail -n 20
./executable show-active 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "summary|status"

# Test stop with note appending
./executable 8 stop "stopping" 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/paused/*.yml | tail -n 30

# Test done with note
./executable 8 done "finished" 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/resolved/*.yml | tail -n 30

# Test remove
./executable remove 1 2>&1
ls /tmp/modtest/pending/

# Test log
./executable log "logged task" +logged project:logproj P1 2>&1
cat /tmp/modtest/resolved/*.yml | tail -n 30

# Test git command
./executable git status 2>&1
./executable git log --oneline -5 2>&1

# Test undo
./executable undo 2>&1
./executable git log --oneline -5 2>&1
./executable show-open 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep -E "id|summary" | tail

# Test open
./executable add "open test https://example.com/path" 2>&1
BROWSER=echo ./executable 9 open 2>&1
./executable 9 note "see http://example.org" 2>&1
BROWSER=echo ./executable 9 open 2>&1

# Test show-tags, show-projects table
export DSTASK_GIT_REPO=/tmp/modtest
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-tags 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-projects 2>&1
./executable show-tags 2>&1
./executable show-projects 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool

# Test show-unorganised: should show tasks with no tags and no project, ignoring context?

./executable context +a 2>&1
./executable show-unorganised 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep summary
./executable show-unorganised -- 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep summary || true
./executable context none 2>&1
./executable show-unorganised 2>&1 | python3 -m json.tool | grep summary

# Test version
./executable version 2>&1

# Test help
./executable help 2>&1 | head -n 100
"}

{"command":"export DSTASK_GIT_REPO=/tmp/table_test2; rm -rf /tmp/table_test2; mkdir /tmp/table_test2; git init /tmp/table_test2; git -C /tmp/table_test2 config user.email "a@b.com"; git -C /tmp/table_test2 config user.name "a"
./executable add "short 1" 2>&1 | tail
./executable add "short 2" 2>&1 | tail
./executable add "short 3" 2>&1 | tail
./executable add "short 4" 2>&1 | tail
./executable add "short 5" 2>&1 | tail
./executable add "This is a very long summary that definitely exceeds typical terminal width and should be truncated in next view but not in show-open view" 2>&1 | tail

echo "=== pty multiple tasks ==="
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable next 2>&1
echo "--- show-open ---"
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-open 2>&1

# Check pty with single id produces detail view always truncated?
echo "--- single task detail APPEARS SAME as list? ---"
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable 1 2>&1

# When would list view appear? Our earlier tests showed list when filtered? Actually when multiple tasks, list.
# When single task ID, detail table (Name Value).
# When no filter and multiple tasks, list table.

# Let's check list truncation: earlier we saw long summary truncated to about 40 chars? Let's see with multiple tasks list
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable next 2>&1 | cat -A | tail -n 20

# So for list view, summary column width is dynamic? Let's add project and tags and due to see columns
./executable 6 modify project:proj +tag due:2025-12-01 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable next 2>&1
# Check widths: header "ID  Priority  Tags  Due  Project  Summary"
# Calculate max widths: ID up to maybe 3, priority 8?, tags comma separated?, due formatted as "2 Jan 2006" or "today"/"tomorrow" maybe? Let's check due formatting in table.
export DSTASK_GIT_REPO=/tmp/table_test2
./executable add "due today" due:today 2>&1
./executable add "due tomorrow" due:tomorrow 2>&1
./executable add "due date" due:2025-12-31 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-open 2>&1

# Explore: show-active, show-paused, show-resolved, show-templates, show-unorganised produce list tables too
./executable 7 start 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-active 2>&1
./executable 7 stop 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-paused 2>&1
./executable 7 done 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-resolved 2>&1

# show-templates
./executable template "tmpl long summary that is also very long and should be truncated maybe" +tmpl 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-templates 2>&1

# show-projects and show-tags - we saw tags list is simple lines, projects table has Name Progress Created
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-projects 2>&1
DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 ./executable show-tags 2>&1

# next vs show-open difference: README says next truncated and default, show-open without truncation
# But our tests show both produce same truncated list for multiple tasks. Could be that next also truncates summary to terminal width, while show-open does not truncate but still list has fixed width? However our earlier test with COLUMNS didn't change. Maybe DSTASK_FAKE_PTY disables truncation logic? Let's try via python pty which truly is a tty
python3 - <<'PY'
import pty, os, subprocess, sys, time
os.environ['DSTASK_GIT_REPO']='/tmp/table_test2'
os.environ['COLUMNS']='80'
# Use pty to spawn
def run_pty(cmd):
    # pty.spawn returns exit status
    import select
    master, slave = pty.openpty()
    proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True, stdin=slave, stdout=slave, stderr=slave, env=os.environ.copy())
    os.close(slave)
    out = b""
    while True:
        try:
            r, _, _ = select.select([master], [], [], 0.5)
            if r:
                data = os.read(master, 1024)
                if not data:
                    break
                out += data
            else:
                if proc.poll() is not None:
                    # drain
                    try:
                        while True:
                            data = os.read(master, 1024)
                            if not data:
                                break
                            out += data
                    except:
                        pass
                    break
        except OSError:
            break
    os.close(master)
    proc.wait()
    return out.decode(errors='ignore')

print(run_pty('./executable next'))
print("---show-open---")
print(run_pty('./executable show-open'))
PY

#   This boolean sets whether deleting tags will be allowed in the
#   repository.  By default they won't be.
# hooks.allowmodifytag
#   This boolean sets whether a tag may be modified after creation. By default
#   it won't be.
# hooks.allowdeletebranch
#   This boolean sets whether deleting branches will be allowed in the
#   repository.  By default they won't be.
# hooks.denycreatebranch
#   This boolean sets whether remotely creating branches will be denied
#   in the repository.  By default this is allowed.
#

# --- Command line
refname="$1"
oldrev="$2"
newrev="$3"

# --- Safety check
if [ -z "$GIT_DIR" ]; then
	echo "Don't run this script from the command line." >&2
	echo " (if you want, you could supply GIT_DIR then run" >&2
	echo "  $0 <ref> <oldrev> <newrev>)" >&2
	exit 1
fi

if [ -z "$refname" -o -z "$oldrev" -o -z "$newrev" ]; then
	echo "usage: $0 <ref> <oldrev> <newrev>" >&2
	exit 1
fi

# --- Config
allowunannotated=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowunannotated)
allowdeletebranch=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowdeletebranch)
denycreatebranch=$(git config --type=bool hooks.denycreatebranch)
allowdeletetag=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowdeletetag)
allowmodifytag=$(git config --type=bool hooks.allowmodifytag)

# check for no description
projectdesc=$(sed -e '1q' "$GIT_DIR/description")
case "$projectdesc" in
"Unnamed repository"* | "")
	echo "*** Project description file hasn't been set" >&2
	exit 1
	;;
esac

# --- Check types
# if $newrev is 0000...0000, it's a commit to delete a ref.
zero=$(git hash-object --stdin </dev/null | tr '[0-9a-f]' '0')
if [ "$newrev" = "$zero" ]; then
	newrev_type=delete
else
	newrev_type=$(git cat-file -t $newrev)
fi

case "$refname","$newrev_type" in
	refs/tags/*,commit)
		# un-annotated tag
		short_refname=${refname##refs/tags/}
		if [ "$allowunannotated" != "true" ]; then
			echo "*** The un-annotated tag, $short_refname, is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			echo "*** Use 'git tag [ -a | -s ]' for tags you want to propagate." >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/tags/*,delete)
		# delete tag
		if [ "$allowdeletetag" != "true" ]; then
			echo "*** Deleting a tag is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/tags/*,tag)
		# annotated tag
		if [ "$allowmodifytag" != "true" ] && git rev-parse $refname > /dev/null 2>&1
		then
			echo "*** Tag '$refname' already exists." >&2
			echo "*** Modifying a tag is not allowed in this repository." >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/heads/*,commit)
		# branch
		if [ "$oldrev" = "$zero" -a "$denycreatebranch" = "true" ]; then
			echo "*** Creating a branch is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/heads/*,delete)
		# delete branch
		if [ "$allowdeletebranch" != "true" ]; then
			echo "*** Deleting a branch is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	refs/remotes/*,commit)
		# tracking branch
		;;
	refs/remotes/*,delete)
		# delete tracking branch
		if [ "$allowdeletebranch" != "true" ]; then
			echo "*** Deleting a tracking branch is not allowed in this repository" >&2
			exit 1
		fi
		;;
	*)
		# Anything else (is there anything else?)
		echo "*** Update hook: unknown type of update to ref $refname of type $newrev_type" >&2
		exit 1
		;;
esac

# When ids.bin missing, original binary assigns IDs based on file creation? Or something else?
# In previous test without ids.bin, IDs were:
# (3, 'task A'), (2, 'task B'), (1, 'task C')
# Creation times: A oldest, C newest. IDs assigned newest first? Let's see: C newest got ID 1, B middle got ID 2, A oldest got ID 3. So reverse creation order.
# Let's test with different ls order? The ls -U (unsorted directory order) is filesystem order, which for ext4 may be hash order, but we saw ls -U gave A, B, C order (creation order). But IDs without ids.bin gave reverse? So not filesystem order.
# Could be that when ids.bin missing, binary scans files and sorts by something like file mod time? But we saw ls -ltr (time sorted) gave A oldest first, C newest last. If IDs assigned in reverse time order, then oldest gets highest ID. That matches our observed IDs: A oldest got 3, C newest got 1. So IDs assigned newest first? That would give newest smallest ID.
# But when ids.bin exists, IDs were assigned in creation order: A ID1 oldest, C ID3 newest. So with ids.bin, assignment is creation order ascending (oldest first gets smallest ID). Without ids.bin, assignment is creation order descending? Or maybe it's binary's fallback: if no ids.bin, it recreates IDs by scanning all files in all status dirs and assigning IDs based on sorted list? Let's test more.

repo="/tmp/id_scan4"

    return subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True, env={**os.environ, "DSTASK_GIT_REPO":repo}).stdout

time.sleep(1)
run(f'./executable add "task B"')

import pty, os, subprocess, select, sys
os.environ['DSTASK_GIT_REPO']='/tmp/mod_prompt3'
def run_pty(cmd, input_data=None):
    master, slave = pty.openpty()
    env = os.environ.copy()
    proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True, stdin=slave, stdout=slave, stderr=slave, env=env)
    os.close(slave)
    out=b""
    # If input_data, write it after a short delay
    import time
    time.sleep(0.2)
    if input_data:
        os.write(master, input_data.encode())
    while True:
        r,_,_ = select.select([master], [], [], 0.5)
        if r:
            try:
                data=os.read(master, 1024)
                if not data:
                    break
                out+=data
            except OSError:
                break
        else:
            if proc.poll() is not None:
                try:
                    while True:
                        data=os.read(master, 1024)
                        if not data:
                            break
                        out+=data
                except:
                    pass
                break
    os.close(master)
    proc.wait()
    return out.decode(errors='ignore')
